articles.title: Entanglement percolation enhanced by the power of choice
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum communication networks are best supported by maximally entangled states, but imperfections in entanglement generation and distribution generally limit the distributed states to being only partially entangled. Therefore, protocols typically consisting of local operations and classical communication are required to create suitably entangled networks. Here, we introduce a power-of-choice (PoC) protocol based on reversing the selection criteria in the Achlioptas process previously considered in classical explosive percolation. The resulting PoC protocol anticipates the entanglement percolation transition, thereby reducing the entanglement resources needed to establish quantum communication. Notably, in contrast to explosive percolation, the PoC protocol admits an implementation using local information with no appreciable loss of performance.

articles.title: Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing via Convex Spectral Design
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fej\'er--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.

articles.title: Symplectic Reck: In-Situ Learning of Gaussian Quantum Operations
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable photonic circuits are a natural platform for physical learning, where hardware parameters are trained directly from measured feedback. We propose a physical learning algorithm and architecture for continuous-variable quantum systems where a photonic circuit is trained in situ to invert an unknown lossless Gaussian quantum operation. We prove that a generic symplectic matrix $S\in\mathrm{Sp}(2N,\mathbb{R})$ admits a decomposition into a triangular array of two-mode symplectic gates on neighboring modes, followed by single-mode symplectic gates. We then introduce the symplectic Reck mesh, which physically realizes this factorization, generalizing the unitary Reck mesh widely used in optical neural networks. When placed after an unknown Gaussian unitary, the mesh is trained in situ by nulling local response blocks one at a time using optical probes and measurements. We identify a local condition number that quantifies the squeezing required for a nulling step and its sensitivity to measurement error. We numerically demonstrate finite-shot training and robustness to systematic gate-calibration errors. Our work extends self-configuring optical networks from unitary to symplectic transformations, bringing physical learning to continuous-variable quantum photonic hardware.

articles.title: Can One Hear the Size of a Clock?
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weyl's law counts the vibration modes that fit into a cavity, and a quantum system with $d$ levels can oscillate at up to $d(d-1)/2$ frequencies without decay. For systems that jump at random between states, no such count was known: they oscillate only out of equilibrium, and the random timing of their jumps damps every oscillation. We find the missing count: if $Q$ is the ratio of frequency to decay rate, a system of $d$ states sustains fewer than $2(d-1)/(\pi Q)$ oscillations whose ratio exceeds $Q$. Nested cycles approach this bound, and measured oscillations reveal how large a hidden system must be.

articles.title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Almost all solutions to vision tasks $\unicode{x2014}$ offered by nature and technology alike $\unicode{x2014}$ rely on capturing an image using a lens or a similar optical instrument, followed by computational analysis by neurons of a brain or a digital computer. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions, where critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage. We address this gap by introducing AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on the incoming photons, learning how to extract the maximum possible information for a given computer vision task from each incoming photon. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array. We train the DONN with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which the discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. We validate the advantage in a noiseless setting as well as a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD with the noise corresponding to $10^4$ photons per single signal photon, where the measurement also learns to mitigate the detector noise.

articles.title: Regev's Reduction Reaches Reconstruction
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Regev's reduction uses a quantum Fourier transform to carry out reductions between various problems related to lattices and codes. We apply it to the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions of certain classical spin glass Hamiltonians, which can equivalently be thought of as cost functions for average-case instances of an optimization problem called $D$-regular max-$k$-LINSAT. This problem becomes hard at low temperature. Here, we use a quantum decoding algorithm called Belief Propagation with Quantum Messages (BPQM) to solve the decoding problem arising from Regev's reduction. Our main contribution is a proof that the minimum temperature reachable using Regev+BPQM is exactly equal to the reconstruction threshold temperature for noisy channels transmitting signals on a tree network. This equality can be understood via Renes' duality between classical and quantum channels, which we use to show that quantum decoding is possible exactly when classical reconstruction on the dual problem is impossible. M{\'e}zard and Montanari identified this reconstruction temperature with a dynamical glass transition predicted by the one-step replica-symmetry breaking (1RSB) cavity equation. It is conjectured that local samplers such as Metropolis Monte Carlo and Glauber dynamics cannot equilibrate efficiently below this reconstruction temperature but may do so above it; our large numerical experiments show close agreement with this prediction across hundreds of different problem parameters. articles.title: Practical Ellipse Fitting for Atom Interferometry
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In differential atom interferometry, it is necessary to extract the differential phase shift between two interferometers that are individually noisy. A variety of techniques can be used for this purpose, under the general label of ellipse fitting. We compare several methods for ellipse fitting, considering parameters and performance relevant to atom interferometry. Statistical, algebraic, geometric and Bayesian methods are discussed, and we describe a novel "reciprocal" geometric method that offers some benefits. Each method has advantages and disadvantages that depend on the use case required. Supplemental material includes basic Python and Matlab code for each method.

articles.title: Dynamical Light-Matter Coupling with Protected Superconducting Oscillators
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting circuits hosting long-lived bosonic modes are an excellent platform for emulating the dynamics of light and matter and exploiting them for quantum information processing. The space of accessible dynamics is greatly extended by introducing the frequency tunability of artificial atoms, whereby the interactions with the light field of a microwave cavity can be modified on demand. However, using external flux bias to control the frequency of transmons introduces significant losses to coupled cavities, reducing their single-photon lifetimes to a few tens of $\mu$s. These imperfections compromise the usefulness of the bosonic mode, which loses its ability to store and manipulate the quantum information of many-photon states. This thesis investigates the issue and demonstrates how to enhance the flux control of microwave cavities without compromising protection. Several hardware solutions were explored, including off-plane remote flux sources routed by a magnetic hose, and lithographically printed on-chip lines equipped with multiple stages of filtering. These developments equip the systems with broadband flux control and photon lifetimes of several hundred $\mu$s. They enable the real-time manipulation of the two central parameters of the Rabi model: detuning and coupling strength. articles.title: Adaptive Protocol for R\'enyi Entropy Estimation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The second-order R\'enyi entropy is one of the most important quantities used for characterizing the entanglement structure of states prepared in quantum many-body experiments. With access to qubit projective measurement data, it can be estimated via a protocol in which repeated measurements are taken after each of a set of random local unitary operations is applied to the quantum state. To obtain accurate values for the second R\'enyi entropy on shot-limited devices, care must be taken when choosing the number of different unitary settings to apply, and the respective number of projective measurements to take. In this paper, we propose an adaptive protocol for estimating the R\'enyi entropy that iteratively optimizes the ratio of basis settings to measurements, using a gradient-based approach and starting from an initial small set of measurements. Using synthetic data, we demonstrate that for several prototypical states, our method converges to values for this ratio that are comparable to the optimal values obtained by a brute-force grid search, and it exhibits slower growth of the measurement budget required for a fixed target accuracy than fixed-ratio protocols. Our adaptive protocol therefore promotes efficient estimation of the R\'enyi entropy in finite-size, shot-limited quantum experiments by making effective use of the available measurement budget.

articles.title: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. articles.title: A trace costs one quantifier: the exact complexity of perfect play in nonlocal games
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a finite nonlocal game, can the players win with certainty? We prove that the existence of a perfect normal spatial strategy is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete, even when restricted to games of value one, so it cannot be decided even with an oracle for the halting problem. This is strictly harder than perfect play in the finite-dimensional and commuting-operator models, which are $\Sigma^0_1$-complete and $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Within the commuting model, the existence of a perfect normal strategy with a finite or semifinite von Neumann host is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete, whereas for every fixed type $\mathrm{III}_\lambda$ subtype it has the same $\Pi^0_1$-complete language as unrestricted commuting play. A trace thus costs one existential number quantifier: the hardness constructions force every perfect strategy to choose a finite clock period or a finite tree depth. Spatial $\Sigma^0_2$-completeness also holds when finite entanglement entropy is required, and both forms are formally verified in Lean. For every computable $0<\alpha<1$, perfect spatial play with $\mathrm{Tr}\,h^\alpha<\infty$ for the reduced density $h$ is $\Sigma^0_2$-complete as well; these conditions form a strict ladder between finite rank and finite entropy. We also prove $\Sigma^0_2$-completeness for one-shot zero-error communication with normal entanglement, and construct a finite channel with zero-error codes of a given size each of which needs infinite entanglement entropy.

articles.title: On the estimation of linear-optical amplitudes and probabilities with entangled input state
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most proposed applications of boson samplers, including photonic machine-learning models, do not use the samples themselves but estimates of output probabilities, marginals or overlaps, obtained to additive precision from a finite number of shots. For product inputs such as single photons, these quantities can already be estimated classically with Gurvits's algorithm and its generalisations. We ask whether entangled inputs change this picture. For any $n$-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension $\chi$, with one photon per site and $L$ modes per site, we give an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an $m$-mode interferometer, whose mean-square error after $N$ draws is at most $\|\psi\|^2/N$ whatever the interferometer, the output pattern and the entanglement of the state. Each draw costs $O(nL\chi^2+nL^3+mn)$ operations after $O(nL\chi^3)$ preprocessing, and an additive error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$ requires $O(\|\psi\|^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ draws, with memory of the order of the input size. The main application is to light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters, such as spin-based sources of photonic cluster states, for which $\chi$ is bounded by the dimension of the source's retained quantum memory: one spin gives $\chi=2$ at any length, and a memory of $k$ qubits, held in emitters or in photons stored in a delay line, gives $\chi\le2^k$, so the cost stays polynomial as long as $k=O(\log n)$. articles.title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.

articles.title: QAOA Inside ADMM: Subproblem Wins Do Not Become Decomposition Wins at Matched Budgets
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We benchmark the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) as the binary subproblem solver in a two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for mixed-binary problems against classical solvers under matched budgets. With 23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem, scoring determines the comparison: on its final readout, the optimized QAOA loses to random search at $n=12$ and 16 binary variables (inconclusive at 20; exploratory and post hoc tests). When credited with its best sample, it wins. In a noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA finds the exact optimum of 97.3\% of planted-family subproblems, against 50.6\%--67.4\% for the four strongest local heuristics (100\% against 90.4\%--94.4\% crediting the four best bitstrings) and a not significantly different 96.5\% for semidefinite rounding with local search (SDP+LS). Under our evaluation-counting convention, its time to solution there is a factor of three to five below the local heuristics' but grows with a larger exponent; it is ten times that of SDP+LS and, in seconds, 54 times that of tabu search with restarts. For the benchmark class, an unconstrained binary quadratic problem in disguise, ADMM's binary step is a proximal step on the reduced problem: at unit penalty ADMM re-solves it, and for larger penalties exact solutions increasingly stall. articles.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

articles.title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention for Static ASL Recognition: A Controlled Study with Parameter-Matched Baselines
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.

articles.title: Initialization masks overcome decoding obstructions in compressed QAOA
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In compressed quantum optimization, a variational state is converted into a classical assignment by decoding noncommuting observables. We show that this step creates structural restrictions that changing the initialization can remove, even when increasing circuit depth cannot. For an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on $n=3r$ vertices, with a fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, every all-plus QAOA circuit has cut at most $2r$, at every finite depth and every real angle sequence. A uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles has expected cut $13r/4$, an additive advantage $5n/12$; an infinite subfamily admits an optimal mask. A second construction retains a linear depth-one separation under weak weighted couplings, a bounded cost-angle domain and a specified production-encoder ordering. Noiseless simulations then test classical mask selection before energy optimization. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieves mean ratio $0.9100$, versus $0.7067$ for the all-plus $X$ baseline and $0.9125$ for the best of $r^2$ separately optimized random masks. On complete cohorts of weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR and Max-2-SAT, the selected mask also improves on the baseline at every size, but it trails the pool at small sizes and leads it significantly only at the larger MaxCut and Ising sizes. Finite-pool order statistics separate the effect of selection from that of drawing a random mask. The results distinguish decoded expressivity from optimized energy

articles.title: Simulating the quantum switch with quantum circuits is impossible
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum switch is a higher-order transformation that combines input quantum channels in an indefinite causal order. Whether quantum circuits can simulate its action, and how many calls to the input channels such a simulation requires, are natural questions about the power of quantum control of causal order. In this work, we prove that no quantum circuit with classically controlled causal order can exactly and deterministically simulate the quantum switch for arbitrary input channels using any finite number of calls. This impossibility holds already for qubit channels and extends to the complete $r$-switch, which coherently controls all permutations of $r$ input channels. These results settle the question of exact deterministic circuit simulation of the quantum switch. They demonstrate that processes with indefinite causal order cannot, in general, be efficiently simulated in this setting even by quantum circuits with classically controlled causal order.

articles.title: A Grover-Amplified Oracle for Maximum Clique on Graph, Minimum Hitting set and Dualizations on Hypergraphs Built on Quantum Phase Estimation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we use a quantum circuit called the Graph Encoding Operator which, applied to the complement $\bar G$ of any graph $G$, yields an oracle for the maximum clique problem suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Analogously, we devise a Hypergraph Encoding Operator which, when applied to a hypergraph $\mathcal H$, yields an oracle for the minimum hitting set suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Interestingly, the latter oracle provides, when measured, an approximation of the number of hitting sets of the hypergraph, thus solving the dualization problem for positive Boolean functions represented in a positive irredundant disjunctive normal form. We give the full construction of both operators, prove their correctness, analyze their complexity, and provide an implementation on a quantum simulator. We discuss the resulting complexity, contrast them with existing quantum computer algorithms based on Grover search and we will show that our algorithms outperform, to the best of our knowledge, all of the previous algorithms on space computational complexity by requiring only $O(N)$ number of qubits with respect to the number of vertices $N$, for representing both graphs and hypergraphs in the encoding operator and, consequently, results in an oracle for both graphs and hypergraphs that uses only $O(N)$ qubits even when the hypergraph contains an exponential (on the number of vertices) number of hyperedges.

articles.title: Demonstration of a partial knowledge quantum key distribution protocol
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.10670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate a novel QKD protocol, named \texttt{Bridge[$d,q$]}, which generalizes the \texttt{SARG04} protocol to $d$ dimensions and $q$ bases. In this protocol, Alice and Bob gain only partial knowledge about each other's raw key. Nevertheless, this partial information is sufficient to distill a definite mutual encryption key. We present an experimental demonstration of the \texttt{Bridge[$2,3$]} protocol. The three unbiased polarization bases were switched using a single Pockels cell. The applied polarization basis switching method is relevant to any 3-basis QKD protocol and to other applications that require fast manipulation of photon polarization qubits.

articles.title: Midbrain somatostatin-expressing cells control pain-suppression during defensive states
articles.summary: In threatening situations, animals exhibit a broad range of behavioral and autonomic responses. As such, a crucial adaptive response is the inhibition of pain, which facilitates relevant defensive behaviors that promote survival. Whereas the structures and mechanisms involved in fear and pain behaviors are well documented, little is known about the precise neuronal mechanisms mediating the emotional regulation of endogenous pain-suppression. Here, we used a combination of behavioral, anatomical, optogenetic, and electrophysiological approaches to investigate, in male mice, the role of somatostatin-expressing cells in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray matter (SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells) in the control of analgesia induced during defensive states. Our data indicate that optogenetic inhibition of SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells promotes analgesia irrespective of animal defensive state. In contrast, optogenetic activation of long-range SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells that project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) abolishes the analgesia mediated by fear behavior. Together, these results identify a novel circuit mechanism composed of long-range SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells projecting to the RVM that regulate analgesia elicited during defensive states.

articles.title: Life-history trade-offs explain local adaptation in Arabidopsis thaliana
articles.summary: Local adaptation has been demonstrated in many organisms, but the traits involved and the temporal and spatial scales at which selection acts are generally unknown. We carried out a multi-year study of 200 accessions (natural inbred lines) of Swedish Arabidopsis thaliana using local field sites and a combination of common-garden experiments that measured adult survival and fecundity, and selection experiments that measured fitness over the full life cycle. We found evidence of strong and variable selection, with particular genotypes favored more than fivefold in certain years and locations. Fecundity showed evidence of classical local adaptation, with accessions generally performing better closer to their home. However, relative to other accessions, southern ones usually had the highest fecundity—but were far more sensitive to harsh winters and slug herbivory, which strongly decreased both survival and fecundity. Furthermore, accessions originally sampled on beaches had low fecundity in all common-garden experiments, but massively outperformed all other accessions in the selection experiments, presumably due to an advantage during seedling establishment associated with their very large seeds. We conclude that local adaptation in A. thaliana reflects strong temporally and spatially varying selection on multiple traits, generally involving trade-offs and different life-history strategies, making fitness difficult to predict and measure.

articles.title: Integral zeros of Krawtchouk polynomials and quantum entanglements
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Heo and Kiem (2019), the authors raised a problem relating integral zeros of binary Krawtchouk polynomials, parametrized by quadruples $(m,n,k,\ell)$ with $m\le n$ and $k\le \ell$, to the existence of pairs of subspaces satisfying the range criterion in quantum information theory, and settled the symmetric case $k=\ell$. In this paper, we solve the problem for the following three asymmetric families: $(m,n,k,\ell)=(3,t^2-1,t(t-1)/2,t(t+1)/2)$, $t\ge2$; $(m,n,k,\ell)=(4,3t^2+2t-1,(3t^2-t)/2,(3t^2+5t+2)/2)$, $t\ge2$; $(m,n,k,\ell)=(4,3s^2+4s,(3s^2+s)/2,(3s^2+7s+4)/2)$, $s\ge1$. The remaining cases are sporadic zeros, with only finitely many for each $m\ge5$.

articles.title: Thermodynamics of Speed and Efficiency with Quantum Feedback
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid thermodynamic operations generally entail irreversible dissipation, giving rise to trade-offs between operating speed and thermodynamic cost. Yet, how quantum feedback fundamentally reshapes these trade-offs remains elusive. Here, we derive a finite-time current--dissipation relation for continuously monitored open quantum dynamics with jump feedback. From this fundamental relation, we establish a quantum speed limit and a power-efficiency trade-off for stationary information engines, identifying how feedback affects state transformations and the performance of engines through both informational entropy and direct dynamical contributions. Our results provide a quantitative foundation for fast, low-dissipation quantum thermodynamics in the presence of feedback control, exemplified by attaining the generalized Landauer bound in finite-time information erasure and approaching unit information efficiency at finite power in the large-system limit of a collective engine.

articles.title: Magic Is in the Eye of the Measure
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magic, or nonstabilizerness, is the quantum resource behind universal quantum computation. Its applications in high-energy and nuclear physics rely almost exclusively on the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (SRE), although magic has no unique measure. For two qubits, we compare the SRE with three measures defined through optimizations over stabilizer states: the min- and max-relative entropies of magic and the logarithmic free robustness. We determine the maximal-magic states of all four measures, with exact proofs, and find that they depend on the measure. In the determination of the weak mixing angle from minimal magic in M{\o}ller scattering, the min-relative entropy gives an energy-dependent value that differs from that of the SRE, whereas the max-relative entropy and the logarithmic free robustness give $\sin^2\theta_W=1/4$ at all energies. We trace this difference to the non-analytic structure of the optimization-based measures. Physical conclusions drawn from extremizing magic can thus depend on the measure.

articles.title: Universality in Quantum Many-Body Spin Ratchets
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a class of quantum circuits, known as quantum many-body spin ratchets, which act on alternating spin chains with two distinct spin types on even and odd sites. This setup breaks parity symmetry and exhibits chiral transport. It has been shown that the drift velocity in the case of integrable, SU(2)-symmetric quantum spin ratchets is universal, and conjectured that the same holds in the non-integrable case. Here, we prove that this universal drift is exact at all times, requiring only translation invariance and U(1) symmetry. Furthermore, we prove that it is sufficient for the circuit to be translation-invariant on average by deriving the same result in the random case. Finally, we demonstrate that breaking translation invariance immediately results in deviations from this universal prediction.

articles.title: Exploring topological signatures of quantum Fisher information scaling in graph states
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph states are a versatile resource for quantum metrology, and their quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a closed-form expression in terms of the underlying graph: it counts pairs of vertices with identical neighborhoods. It remains unclear, however, which global structural properties of a graph determine whether its QFI exceeds the standard quantum limit (SQL). Here we ask whether topological invariants, namely the Betti numbers of the graph's clique complex, capture this behavior, and we address the question numerically with two complementary approaches. First, we randomly add or delete edges in balanced complete multipartite graphs, which combine a QFI beyond the SQL with a single nonvanishing higher Betti number. Edge addition eventually destroys both the metrological advantage and the nontrivial topology. Under edge deletion, by contrast, higher Betti numbers persist well after the QFI has dropped to the SQL. Second, we start from Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi random graphs, whose QFI does not typically exceed the SQL, and maximize a chosen Betti number with a Monte Carlo search. The search drives the graphs toward near-extremal multipartite structures whose QFI lies well beyond the SQL. Our results show that topological optimization offers a route to metrologically useful graph states, but also that Betti numbers alone do not determine the QFI.

articles.title: Harnessing dimensional leakage for continuous-variable randomness certification
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semi-device-independent quantum protocols often rely on strict Hilbert-space dimension assumptions that are difficult to satisfy in realistic implementations, particularly with infinite-dimensional optical fields. The almost-qudit framework addresses this issue by quantifying the leakage of quantum states beyond a target subspace. Although such leakage can severely compromise randomness certification for fixed preparation and measurement inputs, we show that averaging over the full input ensemble can mitigate this vulnerability and extend the range of tolerable leakage. This enhanced robustness enables nonzero randomness certification using low-squeezing single-mode Gaussian states and homodyne detection, thus offering an experimentally accessible continuous-variable implementation.

articles.title: Quantum-enabled measurement of gravitational forces at the milligram scale
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gravity is by far the weakest among all known interactions. While it dominates the large-scale structure of the universe, gravitational interactions between small masses in the microscopic range remain underexplored because they are too weak to be experimentally accessible. The interface between gravity, described by general relativity, and quantum mechanics, which describes the microscopic world, is of particular interest. From a theory standpoint, these two major descriptions of nature have not been combined in a satisfactory manner. Technology is gradually becoming mature enough such that probing gravity at the microscopic scale, where quantum mechanics and gravity potentially meet, is becoming accessible. Explorations towards genuine quantum gravity have to be carried out under conditions where the gravitating masses possess non-classical properties, which necessitates ultimate protection against disturbances, such as ultralow temperatures and a small range of motion. Here, we present an experiment at millikelvin temperatures, where the gravity due to a micron-range coherent displacement of an 87 mg source mass imprints on the motion of an oscillating membrane loaded with a 1.3 mg test mass. Vibrations of the membrane are measured in the microwave optomechanical scheme, which is a key setup for investigating non-classical motional states of mechanical oscillators. When considering the combination of total source and test masses, our setup presents two orders of magnitude progress in sensing gravity at the small scale, as w

articles.title: What are local complementations, really?
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A local complementation at a vertex $v$ of a graph $G$ replaces the induced neighborhood of $v$ with its complement. Local complementations are, at face value, peculiar operations. Yet they famously show up when describing the local Clifford equivalence among graph states, and, because of this, have become a fundamental notion in the study of graph states. Following Bouchet, we show here how local complementations on graphs are more naturally thought of in terms of switchings of (matroid) bases of stabilizer states. Bases and switchings reveal structural properties of stabilizer states that are harder to glean from the graph-theoretic description alone, such as vertex-minors and statistics of local Pauli measurements. Bases also simplify prior proofs about graphs up to local complementations, of which we give several examples. Bases are foundational in the study of (multi)matroids; as such this paper serves as a gentle introduction to the applications of multimatroids to quantum information theory.

articles.title: How Many Shots Does a Quantum Reservoir Need? Measurement Cost and Its Scaling in Buffered Quantum Reservoir Computing
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) inherits from classical reservoir computing the property that only a linear readout is trained, but unlike a classical reservoir its state is never directly observable: every feature is an expectation value estimated from a finite number of measurement shots. The shot budget is therefore a first-class hyperparameter with no classical analogue. Its effect on QRC has recently begun to be studied; what remains unsettled is how a required budget should be defined, and whether competing definitions agree. This paper argues that they do not, and that the disagreement is systematic rather than incidental. This paper distinguishes a \emph{precision budget} $N_\varepsilon$, the shots needed to estimate the reservoir features to a fixed relative accuracy, from a \emph{convergence budget} $N_\star$, the shots needed for the trained readout to approach its own noise-free ceiling. Proposition~\ref{prop:confound} shows that $N_\star$ depends on the noise-free error floor by construction, so that a configuration with a worse floor appears cheaper, and that configurations should therefore be compared at a fixed measurement budget rather than by the budget each needs to reach its own ceiling.

articles.title: Sign-hedged Beam QAOA:Scaling Quantum Optimization Algorithms
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) encodes a combinatorial objective as an Ising Hamiltonian and alternates cost and mixer operations for p rounds. Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) scales further by using the resulting correlations, whether variables tend to agree or disagree, to eliminate variables one at a time. But each inferred sign is accepted irrevocably, so a single early mistake propagates through every later reduction and can discard the global optimum. As elimination proceeds, residuals shrink while effective edge density typically rises, so later decisions face denser Ising problems, a regime that fully connected Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) instances stress test directly. This paper proposes sign-hedged beam RQAOA, which retains the variable or pair selected by standard RQAOA, explores both possible sign assignments, keeps the best B residual problems according to a classical score, and completes each survivor with ordinary RQAOA. On frustrated SK instances, where standard recursion collapses to AR 0.474, beam recovers near-optimal AR 0.998 at the same p. We evaluate the workflow on 50+ instances from HamLib and QOBLIB, spanning 4 and 5 regular and Erdos Renyi MaxCut graphs, Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glasses, and cardinality-constrained portfolio optimization, with up to 60 qubits and hardware runs on ibm kingston and ibm marrakesh. Matched simulator and device cells show consistent beam rankings: simulation and hardware agree that beam recovers near-optimal approximation ratio (AR) where standard recu

articles.title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes $[[n,k,d]]$ with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same $(n,k)$: 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to $4\times10^{13}$ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight $d$. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at $d\ge9$ and $n\gtrsim170$, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs $(n,d)$. The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.

articles.title: Neutral-atom quantum features as complementary structural encodings for graph learning
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural descriptors provide graph neural networks (GNNs) with positional and topological inductive biases. However, widely used classical encodings based on random walks or Laplacian spectra emphasize specific structural statistics of a graph, leaving room for alternative descriptors. Neutral-atom quantum processing units (QPUs) can realize graph-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonians, allowing graph topology to be probed through dynamical correlation measurements. In this work, we use these measurements as quantum graph features (QGFs), providing a complementary, hardware-derived family of structural encoding that is not accurately described by classical features derived from Laplacian and adjacency matrices, even when supplemented with an extended set of random-walk, geometric descriptors and classical physical models. By appropriately selecting the quench parameters of the Hamiltonian, we access two characteristic correlation regimes with distinct structural signatures: antiferromagnetic-like and ferromagnetic-like. On an intrinsic information benchmark of 15 topological and spectral probing tasks, quantum and hybrid quantum-classical features match or surpass classical descriptors on local topological properties. When supplied to message-passing, attention, and graph-transformer backbones, hybrid quantum-classical features yield improvements that are within cross-fold noise on most cells but sign-consistent across architectures. When comparing noiseless, shot-sampled emulation-derived quantum features with a neutral-atom QPU im

articles.title: Kinetic Cluster Embedding for Qubit Decoherence in Dissipative Spin Baths
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpreting the decoherence of a spin qubit requires knowing how the surrounding bath spins behave: whether they fluctuate independently, exchange polarization incoherently, or evolve as coherent groups. These processes can yield the same Hahn-echo coherence time yet produce different coherence signals under pulse control of the qubit. Existing theoretical approaches either capture bath correlations at a cost that grows combinatorially with spin-bath cluster size or neglect polarization transport altogether. We introduce kinetic cluster embedding (KCE), which uses a single dimensionless parameter, comparing the flip-flop coupling of a spin pair with its detuning and linewidth, to decide how each pair must be treated. Pairs that can complete an appreciable exchange oscillation are propagated with the full dissipative quantum dynamics. All other spins are treated as random-telegraph fluctuators coupled through a kinetic network of polarization-transfer rates. We show that for nitrogen-vacancy centers coupled to surface electron spins, KCE propagates about 7 four-spin clusters, compared to more than 10$^5$ propagated by fourth-order master-equation cluster-correlation (ME-CCE4); nevertheless it reproduces ME-CCE4 coherence times to within 15$\%$ for dipolar couplings of order $10^{2}$ times the bath relaxation rate. For a three-dimensional P1 bath, the agreement is within 16$\%$. Coherent multispin clusters emerge as the leading correction to independent fluctuators, and they leave a distinct signature in the CPMG response. Impo

articles.title: From spectroscopy to quantum dynamics: assessing reduced models of a NaCs molecular gate
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how spectroscopic calibration and basis selection affect predictions for a dipolar-exchange gate between two optically trapped $^{23}$Na$^{133}$Cs molecules. We construct a 128-state molecular Hamiltonian restricted to the $N=0,1$ rotational manifold, fit two effective optical parameters to three bright microwave transitions, and compare the resulting spectrum with four additional lines. In the coherent pair model, changing the optical polarization angle by $+0.1^\circ$ reduces the calculated gate fidelity from 94.64\% to 1.09\% at fixed carrier frequencies. Retuning the carriers and restoring the target Rabi frequencies recovers 89.31\%. The remaining sensitivity reflects changes in the multilevel pair dynamics that are not removed by target-frequency and target-Rabi recalibration. Enlarging the molecular basis produces nonmonotonic changes in fidelity, although the 11-state and 25-state calculations give closely agreeing logical maps after phase alignment. Two controls with isolated transfer probabilities near 98.45\% yield complete-gate fidelities differing by more than 11 percentage points. We relate these comparisons to a sufficient bound on the error of a projected propagator. The numerical tests quantify agreement among selected bases for a specified coherent Hamiltonian.

articles.title: Quantum Fluctuations in Noether's Theorem
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When deriving the expression for the Noether's current one obtains a term that is an integral over the Euler-Lagrange equation. This term vanishes along the classical path and so does not contribute to the current. However, quantum particles do not necessarily follow the classical path; this concept is the basis of Feynman's path integral quantization formalism. Thus, for a quantum system, the Euler-Lagrange term does not vanish and, hence, corresponds to a quantum fluctuation of the Noether's current owing to the system deviating from the classical path. Here, we compute this quantum fluctuation from Noether's theorem and the path integral formalism. We find that, for a time invariant system, the expression for the quantum fluctuations is give by minus the functional expression for the Hamiltonian, $\Delta E = -H(y)$, evaluated at the distance from the classical path, $y$. As an example we evaluate quantum energy fluctuations of a single Harmonic oscillator. In the short time limit we recover the energy-time uncertainty relation and in the long time limit we recover the zero point energy of the quantum harmonic oscillator.

articles.title: Shared Lookups and Lazy Residues: Fewer Toffoli Gates for Factoring RSA-2048
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gidney's 2025 construction for factoring RSA-2048 with few logical qubits spends most of its Toffoli gates on discrete-log table lookups and residue uncomputation. We reduce both costs. Shared lookups return entries for several primes of a residue number system at once because they have the same address. Retained intermediate residues remove recomputation during cleanup and enable lazy arithmetic with a single final modular reduction. We prove output preservation and estimate resources with an open benchmark built on the reference simulator. Against the best reference setting within the same logical-qubit budget, using the published model for the reference and benchmark counts for our circuits, we obtain $15\%$ fewer Toffolis at $1{,}461$ qubits ($5.08 \times 10^{9}$ per factoring) and $46\%$ fewer at $1{,}806$ qubits ($2.55 \times 10^{9}$). A matched ablation finds $28.8\%$ fewer Toffolis from three-prime sharing at fixed window and checkpoint settings. Architecture-specific timing determines how much becomes a runtime saving.

articles.title: Time- and phase-resolved emulation of sign-selective counterdiabatic dynamics in a superconducting qutrit
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cyclic three-level systems, phase-sensitive interference can convert a coupling-sign reversal into a population contrast, providing a controllable analogue of handedness. We emulate this mechanism in a superconducting transmon qutrit using two resonant single-photon drives and a phase-controlled effective two-photon drive. Effective loop phases \(\Phi_L=+\pi/2\) and \(\Phi_R=-\pi/2\), separated by \(\pi\), reverse the auxiliary contribution to the dark--bright coupling, canceling the intrinsic nonadiabatic term for \(L\) and reinforcing it for \(R\). Time-resolved trajectories reveal dark-pathway transfer for \(L\) and bright-manifold participation for \(R\). Measured late-time averages give a target-state population contrast of 0.929. Loop-phase measurements establish phase selectivity, while pulse-area and common-mode amplitude scans characterize the operating regime and control sensitivity. These results provide direct time- and phase-domain access to sign-selective counterdiabatic interference in a programmable cyclic qutrit.

articles.title: Optimal Separations Between Randomized and Quantum Query Complexity under Permutation Symmetry
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A function $f:\cD\subseteq A^N\to\{0,1\}$ is \emph{permutation-invariant} if every permutation of its input positions preserves both its domain and its value. We study how this symmetry limits quantum speedups. For $1/6\leq\varepsilon<1/2$, we prove that every such function over an arbitrary finite alphabet $A$ satisfies $R_\varepsilon(f)=O(Q_\varepsilon(f)^2)$, where $R_\varepsilon$ and $Q_\varepsilon$ denote randomized and quantum query complexities with error at most $\varepsilon$. This improves the previous cubic bound (ITCS 2019). We further establish bounds for graph and hypergraph properties, for which vertex relabeling preserves both the promise and the answer. For the same range of $\varepsilon$, we obtain $R_\varepsilon(f)=O(Q_\varepsilon(f)^4)$ for graph properties in the adjacency-matrix model and $R_\varepsilon(f)=O_k(Q_\varepsilon(f)^{2k})$ for $k$-uniform hypergraph properties with fixed $k\geq2$, where the implicit constant depends only on $k$. These improve the previous bounds $R_{1/3}(f)=O(Q_{1/3}(f)^6)$ and $R_{1/3}(f)=O_k(Q_{1/3}(f)^{3k})$, respectively (SICOMP 2024) These bounds are tight for permutation-invariant functions and nearly tight for graph and hypergraph properties. Unstructured search gives a matching quadratic separation with $R_{1/3}(f)=\Theta\!\left(Q_{1/3}(f)^2\right)$. For every fixed $k\geq 2$, we construct explicit families of invariant promise problems on $k$-uniform hypergraphs satisfying $R_{1/3}(f)\geq Q_{1/3}(f)^{2k-o(1)}$.

articles.title: Local distinguishability of five five-partite orthogonal product states
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The local distinguishability of five orthogonal product states (OPSs) has been studied in several multipartite settings, but the five-partite case still requires a systematic characterization. In this paper, we consider five five-partite OPSs, where any two states are orthogonal on exactly one subsystem. By analyzing the distribution of ten pairwise orthogonality relations over five subsystems, we classify the corresponding orthogonality structures by colored orthogonality graphs. After eliminating identical graphs under relabeling of states and permutation of subsystems, we obtain 443 different graphs in seven genuinely five-partite categories. We prove that the OPSs corresponding to 434 of these graphs can be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication (LOCC), while the remaining 9 exceptional cases fall into two types and require separate analysis. Our results give a characterization of the local distinguishability of five OPSs in five-partite OPSs.

articles.title: Optimal asymptotic pure-state conversion under thermal operations
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.08974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum thermodynamics seeks to characterize possible state transformations under thermodynamic constraints in microscopic quantum systems. In the fully quantum regime, however, quantum coherence imposes various restrictions on state conversions, and a complete characterization of state convertibility has remained open. Here we resolve this problem for asymptotic conversions between pure states. Specifically, we show that asymptotic convertibility is fully determined by the free-energy and energy-variance ratios. Our result reveals how genuinely quantum effects quantitatively constrain state conversions in quantum thermodynamics.

articles.title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
articles.summary: Sensory neurons are traditionally viewed as feature detectors that respond with an increase in firing rate to preferred stimuli while remaining unresponsive to others. Here, we identify a dual-feature encoding strategy in macaque visual cortex, wherein many neurons in areas V1 and V4 are selectively tuned to two distinct visual features—one that enhances and one that suppresses activity—around an elevated baseline firing rate. By combining neuronal recordings with functional digital twin models—deep learning-based predictive models of biological neurons—we were able to systematically identify each neuron’s preferred and non-preferred features. These feature pairs served as anchors for a continuous, low-dimensional axis in natural image similarity space, along which neuronal activity varied approximately linearly. Within a single visual area, visual features that strongly or weakly activated individual neurons also had a high probability of modulating the activity of other neurons, suggesting a shared feature selectivity across the population that structures stimulus encoding. We show that this encoding strategy is conserved across species, present in both primary and lateral visual areas of mouse cortex. Dual-feature selectivity is consistent with recent anatomical evidence for feature-specific inhibitory connectivity, complementing the feature-detector principle through circuit mechanisms in which selective excitation and inhibition may together enhance the representational capacity of the neuronal population.

articles.title: Virus-specific impacts on honey bee flight performance are mediated by the octopamine pathway
articles.summary: High annual honey bee colony losses are associated with environmental and biological stressors, including virus infections. In insects, the octopamine (OA) pathway orchestrates the ‘fight-or-flight’ response, regulating energy mobilization, temperature, and flight. We determined that sacbrood virus (SBV) infections induce expression of an OA receptor and enhance honey flight performance, whereas deformed wing virus (DWV) infections reduce flight performance, but how viruses interface with this pathway remained unknown. To elucidate the relationships between the OA response, virus infection, and flight, honey bees were infected with SBV or DWV and exposed to OA, epinastine (EP) – an OA receptor antagonist, or both OA and EP; flight and gene expression were assessed. Pharmacologic manipulation revealed that OA supplementation rescued flight deficits in DWV-infected bees, but diminished performance in SBV-infected bees, while blocking OA receptors altered these effects. Transcriptome analyses indicated that SBV infections, and DWV infection with OA treatment, activated honey bee metabolic pathways, and that SBV-infected bees had greater expression of genes involved in OA synthesis, unless treated with OA. These results provide mechanistic insight for virus-specific impacts on honey bee flight, which may have consequences for foraging efficiency, colony health, and virus transmission.

articles.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

articles.title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

articles.title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.

articles.title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

articles.title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. articles.title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

articles.title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.06996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt deg

articles.title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.07048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development.
